title: Holbein stitch deep dive
subtitle: Two passes along the same line, identical on both sides
excerpt: Holbein stitch is a double-running stitch that leaves the same appearance on the front and back of the fabric. You work the line once as a running stitch, then travel back along the same path filling the gaps. The result is reversible and lies completely flat.
sourceNotes: Caulfeild and Saward, Dictionary of Needlework (1882), Holbein stitch entry. Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776, double-running stitch chapter.

glossaryTerms.definition: Double-running stitch worked along a counted path so the thread looks identical on both sides of the fabric. The traditional outline stitch for reversible blackwork.
A stitch worked by passing the needle in and out of the fabric at regular intervals along a line. Forms a dashed line.
A stitch worked by bringing the needle up one stitch length ahead, then inserting it back at the end of the previous stitch. Forms a solid line.
Ending a thread by weaving the tail under several stitches on the back of the work so it cannot pull out. No knots.

content.text: Holbein stitch
makes the same line on the front and the back of the cloth. You work it in two passes: the first pass leaves gaps; the second pass fills them.
This is the stitch that made traditional blackwork genuinely reversible, valued in an era when embroidered clothing might be displayed from any angle. It is slower than
back stitch
but lies flatter and produces a more refined result. Use it for any blackwork piece where reversibility or flatness matters.
Working a practice piece
Start with a straight horizontal line on 28-count evenweave using two strands of stranded cotton.
Bring the needle up at position A (your start point). Without making a knot, leave a 3 cm tail on the back of the cloth.
Insert the needle two threads to the right at position B. Bring it up two threads further right at position C. You have made one
running stitch
spanning two threads.
Continue along the line in the same way, alternating over two threads and under two threads. At the end of the line you will see a dashed result: stitched, gap, stitched, gap.

Turn the work and travel back along the same line, filling each gap. Bring the needle up at the end of the last stitch you made. Insert it at the end of the gap, emerging at the other end of the gap. The two passes together produce a solid line.
To end the thread, weave the tail under several stitches on the back rather than knotting. See
tying off cleanly
for the detail.
Working corners and diagonals

Holbein stitch handles corners by working to the corner on the first pass, then filling gaps on the return. At a right-angle corner, the first pass carries you along one arm; you turn at the corner and continue along the second arm. On the return, the corner itself needs a stitch that shares the corner hole with the stitch from the other arm. Practice corners on a spare piece of cloth before working them in a design.
Holbein versus back stitch
Use Holbein stitch when the back must be clean, when the piece will be seen from both sides, or when you want a very flat stitch with no raised tension. Use
back stitch
when only the front matters and speed is more important than reversibility.

attrs.heading: Common mistakes
attrs.intro: Holbein stitch is straightforward once you have the two-pass rhythm, but a few things catch new stitchers.

items.symptom: The return pass creates a raised ridge
items.cause: Pulling the return pass too tight, or using too many strands for the fabric count.
items.fix: Keep tension even on both passes. On fine fabric, drop to one strand of stranded cotton.

items.symptom: A gap appears at a corner
items.cause: Not placing the corner stitch so it shares a hole with the neighbouring arm.
items.fix: At every corner, both arms share the corner hole. On the second pass, insert the needle into the existing corner hole rather than beside it.

items.symptom: The back looks different from the front
items.cause: Working back stitch by mistake on the return pass instead of running stitch to fill the gaps.
items.fix: On the return, only enter the holes already used by the first pass. Do not insert the needle into new holes.
